patient.name: Funmilayo Adeyemi
patient.complaint: Sudden severe occipital headache at the gym, 'like being hit with a bat', 8 hours ago
background: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (her mother had a 'brain bleed' at 52)

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a sudden 'worst ever' headache, neck stiffness and photophobia; distractors are meningitis, migraine and subdural. Complication questions hinge on timing.

points: Instant, **maximal** headache at the back of her head.
'The **worst headache of my life**', reached peak within seconds.
Vomited twice; she waited, hoping it would settle.
Arrives in ED at **22:00**, 8 hours later.

steps.lead: Peak intensity within seconds is a **thunderclap headache**: SAH until proven otherwise, however well Funmi looks.
In Funmi, the likely source is a ruptured **berry aneurysm** on the Circle of Willis.
Funmi has three associations: **ADPKD**, a **family history** of SAH and **hypertension**, plus smoking.

points: **Neck stiffness**; she shields her eyes from the light.
No focal deficit; pupils equal and reactive.

steps.lead: Funmi's stiff neck and photophobia are **meningism** from blood in the CSF. Collapse, seizures, low GCS or retinal haemorrhages would mean a bigger bleed.

steps.q: Which feature most strongly separates Funmi's SAH from meningitis?
steps.r: Both cause meningism, but **thunderclap onset** points to SAH. Meningitis builds over hours with fever.

steps.lead: Funmi now faces four threats: **rebleed** (first 12 h), **hydrocephalus**, **vasospasm** (days 7 to 14) and seizures.

visual.title: When each complication strikes
visual.label: Funmi now
visual.caption: Early = rebleed; late = vasospasm. The timing in the stem tells you which.

steps.lead: Watch Funmi's sodium daily: **SIADH** is common after SAH and causes dilutional hyponatraemia.

steps.text: A normal GCS and no focal signs do **not** exclude SAH. Sentinel bleeds can look mild; the thunderclap onset is what matters.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (non-contrast CT) or a normal CT after 6 hours, where the answer is LP at least 12 hours after onset for xanthochromia.

steps.q: Funmi arrives 8 hours after onset. What is the first investigation?
steps.r: **Non-contrast CT head** is always first. It is most sensitive in the first 6 hours, but still the starting point.

steps.lead: Funmi's CT, done at **8 hours**, shows no blood in the basal cisterns. Past 6 hours, CT sensitivity falls.

visual.title: Hours since headache onset
visual.label: Funmi CT at 8 h
visual.caption: Normal CT after 6 hours: LP, timed at least 12 hours after onset.

steps.lead: Funmi's normal CT came after 6 hours, so she has an **LP at 02:30** (12.5 h). CTA follows once SAH is confirmed.

steps.title: CSF at 12.5 hours
steps.text: Xanthochromia and red cells that do not clear across tubes: SAH, not a traumatic tap.

steps.lead: CT plus LP together form the **gold standard** pathway; Funmi needed both.

points: **6 mm posterior communicating artery aneurysm** on the left.

steps.text: Red cells **falling** across tubes suggests a traumatic tap; **xanthochromia** (bilirubin from haemolysis) takes about 12 hours to appear, so it proves an older bleed.
An LP done too early (under 12 hours) can be falsely negative for xanthochromia. And never LP before a CT.

management.exam: Expect nimodipine to prevent vasospasm, coiling as definitive treatment, and warfarin reversal with vitamin K and PCC.

steps.lead: Funmi: ABCDE, analgesia, antiemetic, urgent **neurosurgical referral** and careful BP control to limit rebleeding.
Funmi starts **oral nimodipine** (60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days) on admission, well within the 72 to 96 hour window.

steps.q: How should Funmi's aneurysm be secured?
steps.r: **Endovascular coiling** is preferred: less invasive with a shorter recovery. Clipping is the alternative.

steps.lead: Funmi's PCOM aneurysm is coiled the next morning, within 24 hours, to stop a **rebleed**.
Funmi is not anticoagulated. If she were on **warfarin**: stop it, IV vitamin K 5 mg plus PCC.

visual.title: Funmi's sodium after the bleed
visual.caption: Falling sodium with concentrated urine: SIADH. Treated cautiously; avoid fluid restriction that risks vasospasm.

points: Day 8: new **right arm weakness** and drowsiness.
CT: no rebleed; transcranial Doppler shows high velocities.

steps.text: Nimodipine prevents vasospasm-induced ischaemia; it does **not** stop a rebleed. Only securing the aneurysm does that.

steps.lead: Funmi's care follows **NICE NG228** on SAH, which also sets the CT then LP timings.

science.exam: Applied mechanism: why aneurysms form at bifurcations, why vasospasm occurs late, how nimodipine works, and why SIADH and hydrocephalus follow.

steps.lead: Funmi's aneurysm sat at a **bifurcation** (PCOM junction), where flow stress is greatest and the media is weakest.
Blood burst into Funmi's CSF space: a sudden **ICP rise** gave the thunderclap; meningeal irritation gave the stiff neck.
If Funmi becomes drowsy on day 2, think **hydrocephalus**: blood blocks CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations.
Funmi's falling sodium is **SIADH**: hypothalamic dysfunction drives ADH release and water retention.
Funmi's day 8 weakness came from **vasospasm**, triggered by haemoglobin breakdown products bathing the arteries.
Nimodipine's **cerebral selectivity** relaxes those arteries, improving outcome, but it does nothing for rebleeding.

steps.q: Which kidney condition explains Funmi's aneurysm risk?
steps.r: **ADPKD** is associated with berry aneurysms; screen relatives with a family history of SAH.

mcq.r: A ruptured **berry (saccular) aneurysm** at the Circle of Willis.

mcq.r: **Late vasospasm** at 7 to 14 days; rebleed is early (within 12 h).

mcq.q: Which electrolyte disturbance commonly follows SAH?

mcq.r: Yellow CSF from red cell breakdown (bilirubin).

What is the preferred definitive treatment of a ruptured aneurysm?
Why does vasospasm occur after SAH?
mcq.r: Haemoglobin and bilirubin products trigger **delayed vasospasm**.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the speed of onset is the clue, not the severity alone.

Hydrocephalus: blocked CSF drainage, may need shunt
points.why: Drowsiness with large ventricles on CT.

points.p: SIADH: hyponatraemia
Seizures

points.p: CT angiography to find the aneurysm

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: xanthochromia, not just red cells.

points.why: Distinguishes SAH from a traumatic tap.

points.p: Red cells that do not clear across tubes

Normal or raised opening pressure

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two separate jobs, prevent vasospasm and secure the aneurysm.

points.p: ABCDE, urgent neurosurgical referral, BP control
Oral nimodipine within 72 to 96 hours
Endovascular coiling (preferred) or surgical clipping
points.why: Coiling is less invasive with shorter recovery.

prompts.q: Why do berry aneurysms form, and why does rupture cause thunderclap headache and meningism?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: link each symptom to blood in the CSF.

points.p: Form at arterial bifurcations, Circle of Willis
Weakness in the vessel wall media (congenital or acquired)
points.why: Smoking and hypertension add acquired damage.

points.p: Blood in CSF raises ICP suddenly
Blood irritates the meninges

prompts.q: Explain vasospasm, nimodipine, hydrocephalus and SIADH after SAH.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each complication has one mechanism to name.

points.p: Vasospasm: blood breakdown products (haemoglobin, bilirubin) irritate vessels
Nimodipine: cerebral-selective calcium channel blocker, reduces vasospasm, not rebleed
Hydrocephalus: blood blocks CSF resorption at arachnoid granulations
points.why: Treated with drainage or a shunt.

glossary.SAH: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: bleeding into the CSF-filled space between arachnoid and pia mater.
glossary.subarachnoid space: The CSF-filled space between the arachnoid mater and pia mater.
glossary.berry aneurysm: A small saccular outpouching at an arterial bifurcation, usually on the Circle of Willis.
glossary.Circle of Willis: The ring of arteries at the base of the brain linking carotid and vertebrobasilar circulations.
glossary.thunderclap headache: A severe headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute.
glossary.meningism: Neck stiffness, photophobia and headache from irritation of the meninges.
glossary.Kernig's sign: Pain or resistance on straightening the knee with the hip flexed, a sign of meningism.
glossary.Brudzinski sign: Neck flexion causing involuntary hip and knee flexion, a sign of meningism.
glossary.polycystic kidney disease: Inherited condition with multiple kidney cysts, associated with berry aneurysms.
glossary.ADPKD: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, usually a PKD1 mutation on chromosome 16.
glossary.PKD1: The gene, on chromosome 16, mutated in most cases of ADPKD.
glossary.retinal haemorrhages: Bleeding in the retina seen on fundoscopy, which can accompany SAH.
glossary.rebleed: A second rupture of the aneurysm, most often within 12 hours, causing sudden deterioration.
glossary.vasospasm: Narrowing of cerebral arteries days after SAH, causing delayed ischaemia.
glossary.delayed cerebral ischaemia: Stroke-like deterioration from vasospasm, typically 7 to 14 days after SAH.
glossary.hydrocephalus: Build-up of CSF with enlarged ventricles from blocked flow or absorption.
glossary.arachnoid granulations: Protrusions of arachnoid into the venous sinuses where CSF is reabsorbed.
glossary.shunt: A tube that drains CSF from the ventricles to relieve hydrocephalus.
glossary.SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH: water retention causing dilutional hyponatraemia.
glossary.ADH: Antidiuretic hormone, which makes the kidneys retain water.
glossary.basal cisterns: CSF spaces around the base of the brain, where SAH blood collects on CT.
glossary.lumbar puncture: Sampling CSF with a needle between lumbar vertebrae.
glossary.xanthochromia: Yellow CSF from bilirubin produced as red cells break down, proving an older bleed.
glossary.spectrophotometry: Laboratory measurement of CSF bilirubin and oxyhaemoglobin to detect xanthochromia.
glossary.opening pressure: CSF pressure measured at the start of a lumbar puncture.
glossary.traumatic tap: Blood in CSF from the needle itself; red cells fall across successive tubes.
glossary.CT angiography: CT with IV contrast showing the arteries, used to find the aneurysm.
glossary.posterior communicating artery: Artery linking internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries; a common aneurysm site.
glossary.nimodipine: Cerebral-selective calcium channel blocker that reduces vasospasm-related ischaemia after SAH.
glossary.endovascular coiling: Filling the aneurysm with platinum coils via a catheter to seal it off.
glossary.surgical clipping: Open surgery placing a metal clip across the aneurysm neck.
glossary.interventional neuroradiologist: Specialist who treats brain vessels through catheters.
glossary.PCC: Prothrombin complex concentrate: clotting factors II, VII, IX and X to reverse warfarin.
glossary.transcranial Doppler: Ultrasound through the skull measuring cerebral artery blood flow velocity, raised in vasospasm.
glossary.media: The muscular middle layer of an artery wall.

technique.stem: A 42 year old woman has a sudden severe headache that started 3 hours ago while she was hoovering. It reached maximum intensity within seconds and she vomited. She has never had a headache like it. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 168/96 mmHg. She has neck stiffness and photophobia. There are no focal neurological signs.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis in a sudden headache.

clues: never had a headache like it
steps.x: Thunderclap onset, first and worst, afebrile meningism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thunderclap + meningism + afebrile = **SAH**.

elim: Builds over hours with fever; she is afebrile with a thunderclap onset.
Builds gradually; she has never had a headache like this.
Slow venous bleed with fluctuating confusion in the elderly.
Band-like, mild, no meningism.

steps.x: **C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage.** Peak within seconds is SAH until proven otherwise.

technique.stem: A 51 year old man has a sudden severe headache that began at 08:00. A non-contrast CT head at 17:00 is reported as normal. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. He has mild neck stiffness. It is now 18:00.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: CT angiogram now and discharge if normal
Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset

steps.x: Next investigation after a normal CT.

clues: CT head at 17:00 is reported as normal
steps.x: CT was 9 hours after onset (beyond 6 h) and normal; it is 10 hours now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: LP, but timed at **≥12 hours** after onset (from 20:00) to detect xanthochromia.

elim: CTA finds the cause once SAH is confirmed; it does not exclude SAH.
That is only 10 hours after onset; xanthochromia may not have formed.
Far too late for a possible aneurysmal bleed.
A normal CT after 6 hours does not exclude SAH.

steps.x: **B. Lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset.** CT normal beyond 6 h = LP at ≥12 h.

technique.stem: A 55 year old woman is admitted with a subarachnoid haemorrhage confirmed on CT. CT angiography shows an anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Her GCS is 15, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 152/88 mmHg. She has no focal signs. She is awaiting neuroradiology review.
technique.q: Which drug should be started to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia?

steps.x: Drug to prevent vasospasm.
Confirmed aneurysmal SAH; the lead-in asks about delayed ischaemia (vasospasm).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral nimodipine** within 72 to 96 hours.

elim: A calcium channel blocker, but without the cerebral selectivity or evidence.
For tumour oedema, not SAH.
Only if she has seizures.
Not used to prevent vasospasm.

steps.x: **D. Nimodipine.** Vasospasm prevention = nimodipine; rebleed prevention = coiling.

technique.stem: A 48 year old man had a subarachnoid haemorrhage 9 days ago and his aneurysm was coiled on day 1. Today he becomes drowsy with new left arm weakness. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg. CT head shows no new bleed.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his deterioration?
o: Blood breakdown products causing arterial spasm

steps.x: Mechanism of a late complication.
Day 9, focal deficit, aneurysm already secured, no new blood.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Vasospasm** from haemoglobin breakdown products.

elim: Usually early, and the CT shows no new blood; the aneurysm is coiled.
A chronic process, unrelated to the timeline.
Hydrocephalus causes drowsiness but not a focal arm weakness.
Not the expected complication at day 9.

steps.x: **B. Blood breakdown products causing arterial spasm.** Days 7 to 14 + new deficit = vasospasm.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man collapses at the gym after a sudden, severe occipital headache. He says it felt like being hit on the back of the head. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 62 bpm, BP 178/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. He has neck stiffness and a positive Kernig's sign. GCS is 14.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden occipital 'hit on the head' headache with meningism and no fever is SAH. Meningitis needs fever and a gradual onset.

steps.x: Diagnosis in sudden headache.

clues: hit on the back of the head
neck stiffness and a positive Kernig's sign
steps.x: Exertional thunderclap, 'hit on the head', meningism, afebrile.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Subarachnoid haemorrhage.**

elim: Orbital pain with tearing, recurrent, no meningism.
Needs head trauma and a lucid interval.
Fever and rash, gradual onset; he is afebrile.
Gradual onset; collapse with meningism is not migraine.

steps.x: **E. Subarachnoid haemorrhage.** Thunderclap + meningism without fever = SAH.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has a sudden severe headache and neck stiffness. CT head confirms subarachnoid blood. She has hypertension and bilateral flank masses. Her mother died of a 'brain bleed'. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 172/100 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of the haemorrhage?
practice.e: Bilateral flank masses suggest ADPKD, which is associated with berry aneurysms; they cause most non-traumatic SAH.

steps.x: Underlying cause of the SAH.
SAH plus probable ADPKD plus family history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ADPKD + family history = **berry aneurysm**.

elim: A rarer cause, not linked to ADPKD.
Causes subdural haemorrhage.
Causes lobar bleeds in the elderly.
Causes deep intracerebral bleeds, not SAH.

steps.x: **E. Ruptured berry aneurysm.** Flank masses + SAH = ADPKD berry aneurysm.

practice.stem: A 53 year old woman was admitted 10 days ago with a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Her aneurysm was coiled. Today she is confused, with new weakness of her right leg. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. CT head shows no new blood and normal-sized ventricles.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
practice.e: A new focal deficit 7 to 14 days after SAH with no new blood on CT is delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm.

steps.x: Cause of a late deterioration.

clues: new weakness of her right leg
no new blood and normal-sized ventricles
steps.x: Day 10, new focal deficit, CT excludes rebleed and hydrocephalus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Vasospasm** (days 7 to 14).

elim: CT shows no new blood and it is coiled.
No fever or meningism described.
Ventricles are normal-sized.
No seizure is described.

steps.x: **C. Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm.** Day 7–14 focal deficit = vasospasm.

practice.stem: A 49 year old man is on the neurosurgical ward 4 days after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. He has nausea, headache and muscle cramps. He is euvolaemic. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
practice.e: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urinary sodium after SAH is SIADH.

steps.x: Cause of hyponatraemia after SAH.
After SAH; euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **SIADH**, from hypothalamic dysfunction.

elim: Creatinine is normal.
Would expect hypotension and high potassium.
Causes salt and water loss with hypovolaemia; he is euvolaemic.
Urine would be dilute, not concentrated.

steps.x: **E. Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion.** Low Na, concentrated urine, euvolaemic, after SAH = SIADH.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman is admitted with a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Six hours after admission, before any intervention, she suddenly develops a much worse headache and her GCS falls from 15 to 8. Her pulse rate is 52 bpm and BP 196/108 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
practice.e: Sudden deterioration within the first 12 hours, before the aneurysm is secured, is an early rebleed.

steps.x: Cause of an early sudden deterioration.

clues: suddenly develops a much worse headache
steps.x: Early (hours), unsecured aneurysm, sudden worsening, Cushing response.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rebleed** of the unsecured aneurysm.

elim: Late, at 7 to 14 days.
Would not cause sudden worse headache.
Develops over days, not seconds.
Causes hypotension, not this.

steps.x: **A. Aneurysmal rebleed.** Early sudden worsening = rebleed; late = vasospasm.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man had a subarachnoid haemorrhage 2 days ago. He has become progressively drowsy and his headache has worsened. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 172/94 mmHg. His GCS is 12. Repeat CT head shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles with no new blood.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
practice.e: Enlarged ventricles with drowsiness after SAH is hydrocephalus, from impaired CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations.

steps.x: Cause of drowsiness after SAH.
Early drowsiness with big ventricles and no new bleed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hydrocephalus**: blood blocks CSF resorption.

elim: Would need an infarct on CT.
Too early; typical at 7 to 14 days.
No new blood on CT.
No crescentic collection.

steps.x: **B. Communicating hydrocephalus.** Big ventricles after SAH = hydrocephalus; needs drainage or shunt.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman has a sudden severe headache that started 2 hours ago during sex. She has never had a headache like this. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 156/90 mmHg. She has mild neck stiffness and no focal signs.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

practice.q: Which result most strongly supports subarachnoid haemorrhage?
o: Red cells falling from tube 1 to tube 3

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has a confirmed subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT angiography shows a posterior communicating artery aneurysm suitable for either technique. Her GCS is 15. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 148/84 mmHg.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has a subarachnoid haemorrhage confirmed on CT. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. His pulse rate is 96 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 164/92 mmHg. His GCS is 14.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of his anticoagulation?
o: Continue warfarin and give tranexamic acid
IV vitamin K 5 mg and prothrombin complex concentrate

For a high INR without major bleeding.

steps.x: **C. IV vitamin K 5 mg and prothrombin complex concentrate.** Bleed on warfarin = IV vitamin K + PCC.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has a subarachnoid haemorrhage confirmed on CT 6 hours ago. She is alert with a GCS of 15 and no focal signs. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 146/82 mmHg. She is awaiting CT angiography.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man is given oral nimodipine after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 140/80 mmHg. His wife asks how the drug helps.

o: Blocks calcium channels, relaxing cerebral arterial smooth muscle
Inhibits fibrinolysis to stabilise the clot

steps.x: Mechanism of action.
Nimodipine after SAH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **cerebral-selective calcium channel blocker** that reduces vasospasm.

elim: That is tranexamic acid.
That is aspirin or clopidogrel.
Nimodipine does not prevent rebleeding.

steps.x: **A. Blocks calcium channels, relaxing cerebral arterial smooth muscle.** Nimodipine = cerebral calcium channel blocker against vasospasm.
